verdict: Below average. 2.4L Tigershark MultiAir II is acceptable mechanically but is paired with a poorly calibrated ZF 9-speed automatic (FWD) that is the car's biggest weakness. Poor owner-reported reliability; parts/dealer support thin and repairs pricey. 62k mi is low-mileage for the engine, but the 9-speed risk is age/software rather than mileage driven.
major_issues: ZF 9HP transmission: harsh/delayed shifts, 'drive mode unavailable', slipping, valve body/software issues (CarComplaints lists transmission failure averaging ~65k mi and ~$4k-10k, small sample); oil consumption/MultiAir actuator (solenoid) issues; electrical/infotainment glitches; AC condenser leaks; PTU/rear coupling on AWD only (this car is FWD). 2.4L can burn oil on some units.
risk_reason: Only 62k miles, so most wear items are fine, but the 9-speed is a known failure point and any transmission repair beyond a software reflash/fluid service exceeds $1,000 immediately. As-is with unknown service history; single car, so moderate probability rather than high.
inspect_today: Cold start then drive/shift test if allowed: look for harsh 1-2/2-3 shifts, flare, lurching at low speed, 'Drive mode unavailable' or transmission warning messages. Check ATF level/color/burnt smell (9HP uses specific fluid). Scan for stored codes (P0700/P07xx, P0011/P2xxx MultiAir). Check oil level/condition and for oil on the dipstick being low (consumption), listen for ticking at idle. Check recall status by VIN (9-speed software recalls). Check A/C blows cold, infotainment works, tire wear and CV axle boots.

verdict: Below average to average. The 2.0L Duratec 4-cyl with 6-speed auto and 4WD is a conventional naturally aspirated setup (not the troublesome 1.0L 3-cyl), so it is simpler, but the 6F35 transmission and the 4WD/AWD coupling add some risk. Small, cheap subcompact with decent repair costs; Consumer Reports rates the 2018 about average.
major_issues: Oil pressure warning/low oil pressure complaints (CarComplaints lists as top issue, ~63k mi avg); recall on 1.0L oil pump belt applies to 1.0L only, not the 2.0L; 6F35 transmission harsh shifts/valve body (~$1.5k-3k); rear drive unit/PTU or AWD coupling leaks and noise; exhaust corrosion; tailgate latch/swing-gate and electrical issues; power steering and AC. RepairPal avg ~ $600-700/yr.
risk_reason: A-005 (61k mi) is Low-Medium: young and few wear items due. C-002 (105.7k mi) is Medium: transmission, 4WD coupling/drive unit, and suspension wear start to appear near 100k+, and any one of them can top $1,000. Overall group rating Medium.
inspect_today: Check for 4WD/AWD system warnings; look under the rear for gear-oil leaks at the rear drive unit and PTU; check transmission fluid and for shift flare or harsh 1-2/2-3 shifts; scan for codes; check oil pressure light behavior at hot idle and oil level; inspect exhaust for rust; test swing-gate latch and rear camera; look for coolant seepage and check front struts, bushings, and tires.

verdict: Average to below average for the 2.0L EcoBoost generation (2015-2018 especially). The 2.0L EcoBoost with 6F35 6-speed has a documented coolant-intrusion defect (Ford TSB 22-2229, NHTSA DP26008 investigation) affecting 2015-2018 Edge. The 2020 refresh moved to an 8-speed with a revised engine and is better. 100k-170k miles is where head gasket/coolant intrusion and AWD driveline wear show up.
major_issues: Coolant intrusion into cylinders (misfire, white smoke, low coolant; fix = short block/engine, $4,000-7,000; typically ~60k-150k mi); 6F35 transmission shudder/harsh shift (~$2k-4k); AWD PTU and rear differential leaks/failures (~$1k-2.5k); water pump/thermostat housing leaks; turbo wastegate/boost leaks; cam chain/phaser rattle less common; infotainment (SYNC 3) glitches.
risk_reason: A-021 (2018, 167.6k, AWD) and B-013 (2016, 167.5k, AWD) are High: in the defect window, AWD driveline, and mileage far past where transmission/PTU/coolant issues surface; if coolant intrusion is present, one repair far exceeds the entire $1,000 budget. B-024 (2020 FWD, 104k) is Medium: newer revised engine and 8-speed, FWD, but 104k still risks water pump/turbo accessories.
inspect_today: Check coolant reservoir level and color (low or milky/oily is a red flag); pull the dipstick and oil cap for milky residue or coolant smell; look for white exhaust smoke on cold start and misfire at idle; scan for misfire codes P0301-P0304 and P0300; look for coolant crust around engine block/head and water pump; AWD cars: inspect PTU and rear diff for weeping gear oil; check transmission fluid and any shift shudder; check turbo hoses for oil/leaks.

verdict: Below average. The 1.5L EcoBoost (2017-2019 4-cyl, 6F35; 2020-2021 3-cyl, 8-speed) has a known coolant-intrusion/cylinder-head weakness (Ford TSBs for 2017-2019 with coolant consumption/intrusion; class action alleging coolant leaks into cylinders on 1.5/1.6/2.0 EcoBoost; 2017 recall 17S09 head-crack fire risk is tied to 1.6L). 2020-21 3-cyl has early reports of coolant, transmission and 8-speed issues; also AWD PTU/rear drive weaknesses. 105k-145k miles is the high-risk window.
major_issues: Coolant consumption/intrusion into cylinder (low coolant, white smoke, rough run; fix = short block/head gasket, $3,500-6,000); cracked cylinder head/overheating (1.6L recall, similar designs); 6F35 transmission harsh shifts, shudder ($2k-3.5k); 8-speed on 2020-21 refresh with software/shift complaints; AWD PTU/rear drive unit leaks; turbo failure and wastegate actuator; thermostat housing/water pump leaks; carbon buildup on DI intake valves; spark plug fouling; 1.5L 3-cyl (2020-21) vibration and oil dilution.
risk_reason: Seven cars all at 105k-145k miles, in the window where the 1.5L coolant-intrusion/head-gasket, thermostat housing, and turbo problems appear; the 4WD cars add PTU/rear drive risk. C-033 (143k) and A-023 (144.9k) are the worst, followed by C-003 (114k, 3-cyl 4WD) and the 105k-108k cars. Odds that any given car needs >$1,000 in 6 months are materially higher than average; FWD 2017-2019 cars (C-024, C-034) are a notch lower (Medium-High) than 4WD ones (High).
inspect_today: Check coolant level/color in reservoir (low is the key red flag) and look for sweet smell or crust around thermostat housing, head and hoses; pull oil cap/dipstick for milky sludge; cold start and watch for white smoke, rough idle, misfire codes (P0301-P0304, P0300) and check history; scan for codes; listen for ticking; check transmission fluid and for harsh/delayed shifts; on 4WD, inspect PTU and rear drive unit for gear-oil weeps; check turbo/intercooler hoses for oil; check recalls by VIN (fuel injector, coolant, 8-speed etc.); verify whether coolant-intrusion TSB repair/replacement was done.

verdict: Average to below average. 2013-2016 Escape 2.0L EcoBoost with 6F35 transmission. This generation had many recalls (coolant-related overheating/fire on 1.6L; 2.0L less so) and the 2.0L is generally stronger than the 1.6L. Only 40k miles on this 2015 Titanium 4WD (very low miles for age) is a major plus.
major_issues: Coolant intrusion/leak on 2.0L EcoBoost (TSB covering 2015-2019); thermostat housing and water pump leaks; 6F35 transmission shudder/harsh shifts; PTU and rear coupling leaks on 4WD; turbo wastegate/boost leaks; carbon buildup; door latch and electrical/infotainment (MyFord Touch) failures; low-mileage cars can have age-related issues (aged seals, rubber, battery).
risk_reason: Only 40k miles: most wear items and mileage-driven failures are far off, though age (11 years) can cause leaks and rubber-seal issues. Medium-risk items are 4WD PTU, thermostat housing and MyFord Touch, not major catastrophic failures. Verify mileage (odometer/Carfax) as 40k on a 2015 is unusual.
inspect_today: Verify odometer plausibility vs. wear (pedals, seat, steering wheel); check coolant level/color and around thermostat housing; oil cap for milky residue; 4WD: PTU/rear drive leaks; transmission fluid and shift quality; scan for codes; check for turbo hose oil, intercooler leaks; test MyFord Touch screen, AC, and power liftgate; check tire age and battery; run VIN recall check.

verdict: Average. The 2018 Expedition (4th gen, 2018+) uses the second-gen 3.5L twin-turbo EcoBoost with a 10-speed (10R80) automatic. Generally stronger than first-gen 3.5 EcoBoost (no timing chain issue like 2011-2014), but cam phaser rattle, 10R80 harsh shifts and turbo/intercooler issues are the main concerns. At 114k miles it is in a mid-life window; repairs when they occur are expensive (large vehicle, 4WD, air suspension on some trims).
major_issues: Cam phaser rattle/failure (Ford extended warranty on 2018-2020 Expedition 3.5 through Jan 2023, now expired; fix ~$1,500-3,000); 10R80 transmission harsh shifts, valve body or software, occasionally failure ($2.5k-5k); turbo/wastegate or intercooler condensation misfires; carbon buildup on intake valves (port+direct injection helps in 2nd gen); PTU/rear diff on 4WD; air suspension compressor/struts on Limited/Platinum; 4WD actuator; infotainment; water pump.
risk_reason: One car at 114k miles: cam phaser rattle, 10R80 transmission, and suspension/air ride wear are all plausible, and each repair on this heavy 4WD runs $1,000+; phaser warranty extension has expired so buyer pays. Newer-design engine and no history of widespread catastrophic failure keep it at Medium rather than High.
inspect_today: Cold start listen for a rattle/diesel-like clatter for 2-5 seconds (cam phasers); scan for P0011/P0021/P0014 and other codes; check oil level and condition; transmission fluid and shift quality (10R80 harsh 1-2/2-3, shudder, clunk); inspect turbo/intercooler hoses and charge pipes for oil leaks; check 4WD operation and PTU/rear diff for gear-oil leaks; check air suspension (sagging corner, compressor noise, ride height) on Limited trim; check coolant level and for water pump weeps; check tires for uneven wear; look for maintenance records of oil changes and phaser TSB work.

verdict: Average/uncertain. The 2020+ Explorer (6th gen, new RWD-based platform) with 2.3L EcoBoost I4 and 10-speed 10R60 has a poor first-year record for the 2020 model year (many recalls and quality complaints), while the 2023 is a mid-cycle refresh model. These cars have 162k and 184k miles on 3-6 year-old vehicles, so they were very likely fleet, rideshare, or highway use, which is a mixed picture (steady highway miles are easy on the powertrain but wear everything else).
major_issues: 2020 model year: numerous recalls and TSBs (rear axle bolt, rear toe link, rear suspension, hydraulic brake line, transmission software/10-speed shifting complaints, electrical glitches); 10R60 transmission harsh shifts/valve body and clunks ($2k-4k); 2.3L EcoBoost turbo, carbon buildup, coolant/water pump leaks, fuel injector issues; PTU and rear drive unit fluid leaks and failures on 4WD; infotainment and electrical (SYNC 4 glitches); brake and suspension wear (bushings, control arms) at this mileage. No long-term high-mileage data exists for this generation.
risk_reason: Both cars are at extreme mileage for their age (162k and 184k): transmission, turbo, PTU/rear drive, suspension, and brakes are all due. 184k-mile 2020 (A-017) is worse because of the first-year-model issues and higher mileage; A-013 (2023, 162k) likely has any recalls and warranty history unknown. Little long-term data on this engine at 160k+, so uncertainty is high and tail risk is large.
inspect_today: Run VIN recall check (several open-recall risks, especially on the 2020). Check transmission fluid and shift quality (10-speed harsh/flare shifts, clunk on engagement); scan for codes; cold start listen for turbo whine/rattle; check oil level/condition and coolant level/color; look for oil/coolant leaks at the turbo, water pump, and valve cover; inspect PTU and rear drive unit for gear oil leaks; check rear suspension toe links and control arms for play; brake pads/rotors; tires; check interior wear (pedals, driver seat) for fleet/rideshare use; test SYNC screen, backup camera, and driver assist systems; look for aftermarket tune or collision repair.

verdict: Average. The 2011-2019 Explorer with the naturally aspirated 3.5L Ti-VCT V6 (6F35 transmission) is a proven engine with no turbos, but has well-known weak points: internal water pump (coolant into oil if it fails), PTU leaks on AWD/4WD, and 6-speed transmission wear. 2015 4WD at 93.8k mi is lower mileage; 2019 FWD Limited at 132.7k is solid for age. Note these may be NA 3.5 (not EcoBoost); verify engine at the auction.
major_issues: Internal water pump failure (chain-driven, coolant leaks into oil; $1,200-2,500 engine-out-style repair; typically 80k-150k mi); PTU leaks/failure on 4WD (about $1k-2k); 6F35 transmission shudder/harsh shifts ($2k-3.5k); rear toe-link and suspension noises; power steering/EPAS; cabin exhaust fumes recall (2011-2017, TSB for exhaust leaks into cabin, relevant for the 2015 with kids); 2019 recalls for rear suspension toe link and seatbelt. MyFord Touch infotainment failures on 2015. Timing chain tensioners/carbon on EcoBoost variant only.
risk_reason: B-023 (2015 4WD, 93.8k): Medium due to internal water pump window, PTU, and transmission, plus age-related wear. B-009 (2019 FWD, 132.7k): Medium-Low; FWD avoids PTU, newer, but mileage is high and the water pump and transmission remain possible. A water pump failure that contaminates the oil would be a severe, budget-destroying repair.
inspect_today: Pull oil cap/dipstick and check for milky or coolant-contaminated oil (water pump failure sign); check coolant level and color and for sweet smell or low reservoir; look for coolant leak at the water pump area (front of engine, behind timing cover); check 4WD PTU for gear-oil weeps (B-023); transmission fluid and shift quality; scan for codes; check for exhaust smell in the cabin (rear cargo/exhaust leak TSB); rear toe-link/suspension play; test MyFord Touch/SYNC screen; AC; run VIN recall check.
